## Why this exists

Found while verifying the P-015 mid-turn context hook
([context-injection-audit-2026-07-28](/internal/docs/plans/context-injection-audit-2026-07-28),
D-027 — see also
[why PostToolBatch and not PreToolUse](/internal/docs/agent-insights/coord-mid-turn-delivery)
for the sibling design question that same investigation settled). Two
independent traps compounded to make a genuinely correct hook read as broken,
and both are cheap to avoid once you know they exist — but expensive to
diagnose blind, because each one produces a **confident, silent false
negative**: no error, no crash, just an event that never arrived.

## Trap 1: hooks are read at session birth — a live session never sees a new/edited hook

Claude Code loads `settings.json`'s hook configuration **once, when the CLI
process starts**. Registering a new hook, or editing an existing one, has zero
effect on any session that is already running — not after one turn, not after
a hundred. This applies equally to a **probe** hook you add purely to test
whether an event fires, and to the **real** hook you're trying to fix: if you
edit either while a session is live, every turn you drive in that session is
testing the *old* (or nonexistent) configuration, not the one on disk.

**Consequence for verification:** any hook check requires a session **started
after** the settings change — `psu`/`claude` launched fresh, not a resumed or
already-open one. This is easy to get backwards when you're mid-debug in an
existing session and just want a quick answer without restarting anything;
that quick answer will be wrong.

## Trap 2: `claude -p` never fires `PostToolBatch` — even when the triggering tool call demonstrably ran

Headless one-shot mode (`claude -p "..."`) is the obvious low-disturbance way
to test a hook: no live session to interrupt, a clean process, a single
prompt/response. For `PostToolBatch` specifically, it does not work.

**What was observed:** a `claude -p` run that unambiguously executed the Bash
tool — its final answer echoed back the exact stdout of the command it ran —
produced **zero** `PostToolBatch` hook invocations. The hook's HTTP endpoint
was never hit. In the **same run**, the `UserPromptSubmit` hook fired
normally and its injected marker text was visible in the model's reply. So
this is not "hooks don't run under `-p`" in general — it is specific to the
`PostToolBatch` event class.

**Why this reads as "my hook is broken" when it isn't:** the natural next
move is to assume the hook script itself has a bug, or that `PostToolBatch`
was the wrong event to register for and rewrite the mechanism onto
`PreToolUse` instead. Both ends were checked independently and both work:

- A throwaway `PostToolBatch` probe hook, registered in `~/.claude/settings.json`
  and exercised from an **interactive** psu session (started after
  registration, per Trap 1), *did* capture a real payload — a genuine
  `tool_calls` entry for `mcp__papercusp-su__work_items_claim`.
- The real hook (`posttoolbatch-midturn-context.sh`), driven by hand with a
  realistic `PostToolBatch` JSON payload piped to its stdin, POSTs correctly
  to the mid-turn-context endpoint and emits the right
  `hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext` — exit 0, end to end.

Both halves of the pipeline are correct. Only the `-p` **driver** never
fires the event — so `-p` produces a false negative that would send someone
"fixing" a hook that already works, or — worse — moving it to `PreToolUse`,
where it genuinely cannot deliver `additionalContext` without also voting on
tool permission (see the design note this doc links above).

## The verification method that does work: a path-distinct stub marker, from a freshly-started interactive session

Combine the two fixes:

1. **Register (or edit) the hook, then start a brand-new interactive session**
   (`psu` / `claude`, not `-p`, not a resume) — this is the only session type
   guaranteed to have read the current `settings.json` (Trap 1).
2. **Make the hook write a marker whose path is unique to this test run** (a
   throwaway probe hook, or a temporary line added to the real one) — e.g.
   append the event payload to a file named with a fresh UUID/timestamp,
   rather than a fixed path a stale prior run could have already populated.
   The path-distinctness matters: a fixed marker path can't tell a fresh
   real firing apart from a leftover file from an earlier, unrelated test.
3. **Drive the session through a real turn that exercises the event** (a tool
   call for `PostToolBatch`, a fresh prompt for `UserPromptSubmit`, etc.) and
   check the marker file afterward.
4. **Independently confirm the consuming side** by feeding the real hook a
   realistic payload by hand (`echo '<payload>' | ./the-hook.sh`) and
   checking its own exit code / output — this isolates "does the event
   reach the hook" from "does the hook do the right thing once invoked,"
   which is exactly the split that resolved this investigation.

## Cost if you skip this

This investigation burned several verification runs before landing on the
method above — each `-p` run confidently reported "the hook didn't fire,"
which is true of `-p` and says nothing about the hook. Cheap to avoid once
written down; expensive to rediscover per-agent.
